words:
• CRB: the Arm Phoenix Reference Server in our lab, 128 cores (Arm part 0xd83), one NUMA node.
  • ASCT: the Arm System Characterization Tool, version 0.7.1+77461b3. It is Arm's tool for memory latency and bandwidth tests.
  • read loop: the few instructions that a benchmark repeats to read a buffer. This report compares three read loops.
  • old read: the read loop of our benchmark before 2026-11-13. It loads every byte and adds the loaded values.
  • new read: the read loop of our benchmark since 2026-11-13. It loads every byte and does no other work. Its values here are those of the assembly form (asmread) unless a line says otherwise.
  • ASCT read: the read loop of ASCT (function my_read_no_nops_rep_64b). It loads 8 bytes of each 64-byte line.
  • line: one 64-byte cache line. Caches and memory move data in lines.
  • L1, L2: the two private caches of a core, 64 KiB and 2 MiB.
  • SLC: the system-level cache, 128 MiB, shared by all cores. Linux calls it L3.
  • mesh: the on-chip network that links cores, SLC and memory ports. CRB has two meshes: mesh 0 holds CPUs 0 to 63, mesh 1 holds CPUs 64 to 127.
  • 64+56: 64 threads on CPUs 0 to 63 and 56 threads on CPUs 64 to 119, one thread per CPU, 256 MiB per thread.
  • injected NOPs (N): an ASCT option (--bw-fine-delay N). ASCT then runs an empty loop of N rounds after each load. ASCT calls the rounds NOPs. One round has 3 instructions.
  • window: the instructions that a core holds in flight at one moment. A read loop with few instructions per line puts many lines into one window.
  • prefetcher: the part of a core that requests lines before the program asks for them.
  • core counter: a hardware counter inside a core, for example cycles or cache refills. ASCT reads them through its capture code named dietperf.
  • probe build: the variant of the ASCT benchmark binary that contains the capture code.
  • mesh counter: a hardware counter of the mesh (Linux units arm_cmn_0 and arm_cmn_1). Reading it needs root.
  • L2 refill: one line that enters L2 from the SLC or from memory. The counter is l2d_cache_refill.
  • long-latency miss: a load that had to wait for its line. A load whose line was prefetched in time is not counted.
  • L1 prefetches, L2 prefetches: the counts of the counters l1d_cache_hwprf and l2d_cache_hwprf. One count is one request of the hardware prefetcher of that cache.
  • busy level: a number from 0 to 3 that the mesh sends to a core with each answer. 3 means most busy. The core counts the answers of each level (counters l2_chi_cbusy0 to l2_chi_cbusy3).
  • hop: one step from one crosspoint of the mesh to the next.
  • slow state: the condition at 64+56 in which a thread reads about 2 GB/s. In the fast condition it reads about 5 GB/s.
  • lower bound of a total: all bytes that the threads of one process read, divided by the time of the slowest thread. ASCT itself adds the rates of the threads.
  • huge page: a memory page of 2 MiB or more. A normal page has 4 KiB. With transparent huge pages the kernel gives huge pages to a program that did not ask for them.
  • P-A1, R-A3, D-A2 and similar names: the predictions (P), rules (R) and descriptive items (D) of the decisions file. They were written before the data that they judge.
  • part U, N, C, NC: the four parts of the one-core runs. U: no counters. N: injected NOPs, no counters. C: counters. NC: injected NOPs with counters.
  • marker file: the file /tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING on CRB. The other user of CRB creates it while his tests run.
  • process: one start of the ASCT benchmark binary. It prints one rate.
  • median, range: the middle value of the processes of a cell, and the smallest to the largest value.
  • GB: 109 bytes. KiB, MiB, GiB: 210, 220, 230 bytes.
  • Arm reference machines A0 and A1: the two machines of the vendor baseline runs in the Arm welcome kit. They have firmware v0.9.0 and two NUMA nodes.
  • NUMA node: a group of cores and the memory that the firmware declares as local to them.
  • block: a time window that Jeremy Conner reserves on CRB in Slack channel #phoenix-crb.
  • est.: an estimate, not a measurement.
asked: Two results of our own read benchmark on CRB are not understood.

• Question 1, 8 MiB. The new read loop is 27.0 % faster than the old read loop at 1 MiB on one core. At 8 MiB the gain was 0.78 % in the first run of 2026-11-13 [Ref1]. The runs of 2026-11-15 found 0.2 to 6.7 % [Ref2].
  • Question 2, whole chip. At 64+56 threads the old read loop reads 465.5 to 470.1 GB/s in total. The new read loop reads 288.5 to 309.8 GB/s [Ref3].

The request for this work: repeat both tests with ASCT on the same cores and sizes, compare the rates with the old and the new loop, and capture the counters and registers that ASCT can reach, with a focus on the prefetchers.
cap_path: Figure 1. The ASCT front end fixes its core and needs huge pages. So the runs called the ASCT benchmark binary directly, with the command line that the front end builds.
cap_loops: Figure 2. The ASCT loop loads one eighth of the bytes that it counts. Its rate is comparable with ours only when the transfer of lines is the limit, not the work inside the core.
refs: [Ref1] First run of the new loops, 2026-11-13: crb/results/kernels-20261113T181222Z/one-thread.csv and threads120.csv. The gain uses the medians of 6 repetitions on CPU 2.
[Ref2] The 8 MiB work of 2026-11-15: crb/new-test-kernel/tackle-8mb-results.md. Numbers from tackle-8mb-analysis/final8.json, blocks size_curve, ZS, evict (step ZC) and prefetch (step YC).
[Ref3] The whole-chip work of 2026-11-15: crb/tmp/agent-scratch/w120-2026-11-15/FINDINGS.md, sections F2 to F4. Report crb/new-test-kernel/whole-chip-read-drop.html.

[Ref4] ASCT source, tarball ~/asct/asct-0.7.1+77461b3/asct-0.7.1+77461b3.tar.gz on CRB: src/core/recipes/impl/memory_load_latency.py and recipe_benchmark_base.py (choice of CPUs), src/core/recipes/configuration/schema.py (user settings), src/core/benchspec/memory_benchspec.py (command line).

[Ref6] ASCT counter and register code in the same tarball: extern/dietperf/dietperf.h, src/core/asct_pmu_api.py, src/core/asct_env.py, src/core/config/ubench.json, src/core/recipes/impl/sysreg.py, src/core/recipes/impl/cmn.py, src/lib/cmn-tools/cmn_api.py.

[Ref11] Vendor baseline runs: vendor-resources/ARM/agi-cpu-welcome-kit/tools/asct/reports/ (two console outputs and two result archives). The file raw/bandwidth-sweep/bandwidth-sweep.ubench.json of each archive holds the one-core sweep.

how: The ASCT front end (the command asct run) could not be used on CRB as it is. There are four reasons.

• Fixed core. The ASCT benchmark bandwidth-sweep takes its one core from the code: the last CPU of NUMA node 0. On CRB that is CPU 127 [Ref4]. CPU 127 is isolated and must not be used [Ref13].
  • All CPUs. The ASCT benchmark peak-bandwidth uses every CPU of the node. On CRB that includes CPUs 120 to 127. Our runs may use CPUs 0 to 119 only [Ref4] [Ref13].
  • Huge pages. Both benchmarks first run the ASCT benchmark latency-sweep, which needs huge pages. CRB has 0 free huge pages. Adding huge pages needs root and changes a system setting [Ref7] [Ref10].
  • One user setting. bandwidth-sweep has one user setting, cycle_base. It has no setting for the core or for the buffer sizes [Ref4].
So each run started the ASCT benchmark binary directly. The command line is the one that the front end builds [Ref4]:

numactl --membind 0 loaded-latency-asct-sve.bin --duration D --delay-seconds 0 \
    --bw-cpu C [--bw-cpu C ...] --bw-buflen BYTES --bw-fine-delay N --bw-write=0 --bw-cacheline-bytes 64

• D is the length of the measured phase in seconds. The ASCT default is 0.25 s.
  • C is a CPU. One thread runs on each CPU that the command line names.
  • BYTES is the buffer size of each thread.
  • N is the number of injected NOPs.
What is the same as in a run through the front end, and what is not:

• Same binary. Runs without counters used the binary that the ASCT installer built on CRB [Ref10].
  • Same loop in the counted runs. Runs with counters used the probe build. It was built on CRB from the ASCT source archive, with the compiler flags of the ASCT configuration file [Ref6] [Ref9]. The machine code of the two ASCT read functions is identical in both binaries. A rebuild without the probe flag gave a file with the same SHA-256 sum as the installed binary (first 8 digits e26babf6) [Ref10].
  • Timing. One-core runs used the ASCT default of 0.25 s. Whole-chip runs used 2 s. Three whole-chip processes used 0.25 s as a check.
  • Pages. The ASCT bandwidth code allocates its buffer with posix_memalign and does not ask for huge pages [Ref5]. The CRB kernel setting for transparent huge pages is "always". A 64 MiB test buffer on CRB was backed by 2 MiB pages for all of its 64 MiB [Ref10]. The Arm reference machines record the setting "madvise" [Ref11]. So their buffers used 4 KiB pages (est. from the setting, not measured).
  • Different by design. The CPUs, the buffer sizes and the thread layout are ours, not those of the front end.
loops:
• Old read. It loads all 64 bytes of a line with 2 pair-load instructions (ldp q, 32 bytes each). Then it adds the loaded values with 4 vector add instructions [Ref3].
  • New read. It loads all 64 bytes of a line with 2 ldp q instructions. It does no other work [Ref3].
  • ASCT read. It loads the first 8 bytes of a line with 1 load instruction (ldr x). It does no other work. One loop round covers 8 lines and has 3 more instructions for the loop itself [Ref5]. The counters give 1.375 instructions per line.
  • ASCT read with N injected NOPs. ASCT then uses the function my_read. It loads 8 bytes of a line and then runs an empty loop of N rounds [Ref5].
  • All three count 64 bytes per line. So a rate in this report is a rate of lines: 64 GB/s is 1.0 × 109 lines per second for each loop.
The machine code of the ASCT read loop on CRB, from the installed binary (8 loads, then 3 loop instructions):

The window of a loop matters for question 2. The work of 2026-11-15 estimated how many lines one window covers: 18 to 22 lines for the old read loop and 36 to 40 lines for the new read loop [Ref3]. The ASCT read loop has fewer instructions per line than both. So its window covers more lines than that of the new read loop (est., not measured for this loop).
capture: The request asked for every counter and register that ASCT can capture. ASCT has four ways. One gave data without root. The other three need root or a kernel module, and they gave nothing in this work.

• Core counters: captured. The probe build contains the ASCT capture code named dietperf. It reads a list of raw event codes from the environment variable DIETPERF_PMUv3 [Ref6]. It counts in user mode. It counts only the measured phase of each thread. It needs no root. This work counted 43 events in 7 sets of 7 [Ref9]. The sets include the 9 prefetch events that CRB lists for the data caches: 4 for the hardware prefetchers and 5 for prefetch instructions. Not counted: 2 events for address-translation work caused by prefetch instructions, and the events of the instruction cache.
  • The front-end switch for core counters: not used. The switch ASCT_DEBUG_ENABLE_PMU=1 selects a fixed list of events. That list holds no prefetch event [Ref6]. So the runs passed their own event codes to the capture code.
  • Mesh counters: not captured. The ASCT capture code has a setting for mesh counters (DIETPERF_CMN). It opens them as system-wide events [Ref6]. CRB allows system-wide events to root only (the kernel setting perf_event_paranoid is 2) [Ref10]. So the benchmark itself would have to run as root. The plan was to read the same kernel counters with the Linux command perf stat -a as root, while the benchmark runs without root. That root command was refused by the permission system of this agent session.
  • Core registers: not captured. The report asct report sysreg needs a kernel module that shows registers under /sys/kernel/sysreg. CRB has no such folder [Ref10]. The ASCT source lists three core types for this report (Neoverse N1, N2 and V2). The core type of CRB is not in that list [Ref6].
  • Mesh registers: not captured. The report asct report cmn reads the mesh registers through /dev/mem as root [Ref6]. Its option --detect also puts a load on every CPU in turn, which includes the isolated CPUs 126 and 127. No root command ran in this work. So this report was not run. The layout of the mesh is known from the kernel record of 2026-11-02 [Ref14].

Insufficient data on the prefetcher settings. No run of this work read a control register of a prefetcher. The measurement that would resolve it: the register report of ASCT after Arm supplies the kernel module with support for this core type, or a statement from Arm on the prefetcher settings of firmware v0.7.2.
q1_intro: The runs of this section use one thread on one CPU. One process gives one rate.

• ASCT read: 16 buffer sizes on CPUs 2 and 41, 8 processes per size and CPU, measured phase 0.25 s [Ref9] [Ref10].
  • Old read and new read: the values of 2026-11-15 on the same two CPUs [Ref2]. They were not run again in this work.
  • Load of CRB: the 1-minute load average at the start of the 800 processes was 0.08 to 1.22. At most 3 tasks were runnable. A load near 1 is the test itself (est.) [Ref10].
cap_size: Figure 3. Up to 2.5 MiB the ASCT read loop is the fastest of the three loops. From 3 MiB to 32 MiB it is slower than the new read loop. From 4 MiB to 32 MiB it is the slowest of the three (CPU 2).
cap_fall: Figure 4. Both load-only loops lose rate from 1 MiB to 8 MiB. The ASCT loop loses 40 %, the new read loop 17 % (CPU 2). The old read loop keeps its rate. The Arm reference machines show the same fall of the ASCT loop.
q1_rates:
• The ASCT loop loses about 40 % from 1 MiB to 8 MiB. It reads 95.9 GB/s at 1 MiB and 57.2 GB/s at 8 MiB on CPU 2 and 95.3 GB/s at 1 MiB and 58.1 GB/s at 8 MiB on CPU 41 [Ref10].
  • Prediction P-A1 holds on both CPUs. It said that the ratio of the two rates is below 0.90. The ratio is 0.596 on CPU 2 and 0.609 on CPU 41 [Ref8].
  • The Arm reference machines show the same fall. The ASCT loop reads 93.1 and then 57.3 GB/s on machine A0 (ratio 0.616). It reads 106.5 and then 63.5 GB/s on machine A1 (ratio 0.596). Each value is one process of the vendor run [Ref11].
  • Our loops for comparison. The new read loop reads 85.2 GB/s at 1 MiB and 71.0 GB/s at 8 MiB on CPU 2 (ratio 0.833). The old read loop reads 67.1 and 67.0 GB/s (ratio 0.999) [Ref2].
  • The order of the loops turns around. At 1 MiB the order on CPU 2 is ASCT read (95.9 GB/s), new read (85.2), old read (67.1). At 8 MiB it is new read (71.0), old read (67.0), ASCT read (57.2).
  • The ASCT loop shows one rate at 8 MiB. Its 8 processes lie within 57.18 to 57.25 GB/s on CPU 2 and 58.03 to 58.08 GB/s on CPU 41. On 2026-11-15 the new read loop moved between two rates at 8 MiB: about 67.5 and 71.1 GB/s on CPU 2, about 69.1 and 71.6 GB/s on CPU 41 [Ref2].
  • No step at 8 MiB. The ASCT rate falls at every size step from 2 MiB to 32 MiB on both CPUs. The fall from 6 MiB to 8 MiB is 2.33 GB/s on CPU 2 and 2.36 GB/s on CPU 41. The fall from 8 MiB to 12 MiB is 2.10 GB/s on CPU 2 and 2.15 GB/s on CPU 41.
q1_cost_intro: The counted runs use the probe build and the ASCT capture code. Each cell has 2 processes per event set. Every value below is a count per 64-byte line of the measured phase [Ref6] [Ref9].

• L2 refills per line is the share of lines that enter L2 from outside, which means from the SLC or from memory. The work of 2026-11-15 named it r.
  • Check of the counted runs. The rate of the counted processes differs from the rate of the uncounted processes by at most 0.9 % on CPU 2 and 1.0 % on CPU 41 over the 16 sizes.
  • Clock. Cycles per line times lines per second gives 2.798 to 2.799 GHz on CPU 2 and 2.798 to 2.799 GHz on CPU 41 at every size.
cap_cost: Figure 5. Both load-only loops cost more cycles when more lines come from outside L2. The ASCT loop pays about 1.76 cycles for such a line, the new read loop about 0.66 cycles (CPU 2).
q1_cost:
• Fitted cost of the ASCT loop (item D-A2 of the decisions file). Cycles per line = 1.69 + 1.76 × r (largest distance of a point from the line: 0.14 cycles) on CPU 2 and 1.71 + 1.69 × r (largest distance of a point from the line: 0.12 cycles) on CPU 41, over the 13 sizes from 1 to 32 MiB [Ref8] [Ref10].
  • Fitted cost of the new read loop on 2026-11-15. Cycles per line = 2.09 + 0.66 × r on CPU 2 and 2.08 + 0.65 × r on CPU 41 [Ref2].
  • The ASCT loop is cheaper while the lines come from L2. Its fixed cost is 1.69 cycles per line against 2.09 for the new read loop (CPU 2). It has half the instructions per line.
  • The ASCT loop pays more for a line from outside L2. It pays 1.76 cycles against 0.66 for the new read loop (CPU 2). That is 2.7 times as much.
  • Both loops take the same share of lines from outside L2. At 8 MiB r is 0.815 for the ASCT loop and 0.827 for the new read loop (CPU 2). So at this size r is almost the same for both loops.
  • Cost at 8 MiB. The ASCT loop needs 3.13 cycles per line, the new read loop 2.52, the old read loop 2.67 (CPU 2) [Ref2] [Ref10].
q1_pf_intro: CRB lists 9 prefetch events for the data caches. All 9 were counted at all 16 sizes on both CPUs [Ref9] [Ref10].

• l1d_cache_hwprf, l2d_cache_hwprf: prefetches of the hardware prefetcher of L1 and of L2.
  • l2d_cache_l1hwprf, l2d_cache_refill_l1hwprf: L2 accesses and L2 refills that the L1 prefetcher caused.
  • 5 events for prefetch instructions (l1d_cache_prfm, l1d_cache_refill_prfm, l2d_cache_prfm, l2d_cache_refill_prfm, prf_spec). All 5 are 0 at every size. The ASCT loop holds no prefetch instruction.
  • l1d_cache_lmiss_rd, l2d_cache_lmiss_rd: long-latency read misses of L1 and of L2. They show the result of prefetching: a line that arrived in time causes no long-latency miss.
cap_prefetch: Figure 6. No counter changes its course at 8 MiB (the vertical line). L2 long-latency read misses rise from 0.01 per line at 1 MiB to 0.32 per line at 8 MiB (CPU 2).
q1_pf:
• Rule R-A3: no prefetch counter is different at 8 MiB. The rule compares the value at 8 MiB with the values at 6 MiB and 12 MiB on both CPUs [Ref8]. So these counters give no sign that a prefetcher behaves differently at 8 MiB than at the neighbour sizes.
  • The L1 prefetcher does almost nothing for the ASCT loop. At 8 MiB it makes 0.009 prefetches per line on CPU 2 and 0.009 prefetches per line on CPU 41. Every line is an L1 long-latency miss: 0.99 per line at 8 MiB and 1.00 per line at 1 MiB (CPU 2).
  • The new read loop had fewer L1 long-latency misses. On 2026-11-15 it had 0.29 per line at 1 MiB and 0.34 per line at 8 MiB (CPU 2, steps YC and ZC) [Ref2].
  • The L2 prefetcher works for the ASCT loop, and it is late for a part of the lines. It makes 1.54 prefetches per line at 8 MiB (CPU 2). The loop still has 0.321 L2 long-latency read misses per line on CPU 2 and 0.321 L2 long-latency read misses per line on CPU 41. That is 39 % and 39 % of the L2 refills.
  • For the new read loop the L2 prefetcher was in time. On 2026-11-15 the new read loop had at 8 MiB 0.0005 L2 long-latency read misses per line on CPU 2 and 0.0006 L2 long-latency read misses per line on CPU 41 (step ZC) [Ref2].
  • The part that grows with the size is the late lines. L2 long-latency read misses per line of the ASCT loop on CPU 2: 0.013 at 1 MiB, 0.255 at 4 MiB, 0.321 at 8 MiB, 0.358 at 32 MiB.

Hypothesis (not proven by the counters above). The ASCT loop has 1.375 instructions per line, and the new read loop has 2.75. So one window of the ASCT loop covers more lines. Its loads ask for lines that the L2 prefetcher has not fetched yet. The test for this hypothesis is the ASCT loop with injected NOPs, which follows.
q1_pad_intro: Injected NOPs slow the ASCT loop down by a known amount. With N injected NOPs the loop has 6 + 3 × N instructions per line. The counters give 9.0, 12.0 and 18.0 instructions per line for N = 1, 2 and 4 [Ref5] [Ref10].

• Part N, no counters: 1, 2, 4 and 8 injected NOPs at 32 KiB, 1 MiB and 8 MiB, 4 processes per CPU and cell [Ref9].
  • Part NC, with counters: 1, 2 and 4 injected NOPs at 1 MiB and 8 MiB, 6 processes per CPU and cell (2 for each of 3 event sets). This part was defined after the first data. Its prediction P-A5 was written before its own data [Ref8].
  • Load of CRB for part NC: 1-minute load average 1.14 to 1.25 at the start of the 72 processes, at most 2 runnable tasks [Ref10].
cap_pad: Figure 7. With 1 or 2 injected NOPs the ASCT loop reads 8 MiB faster than without NOPs: 64.8 and 69.0 GB/s against 57.2 GB/s (CPU 2). With 4 or 8 injected NOPs the NOPs are the limit at both sizes.
q1_pad:
• The padded loop reads 8 MiB faster. Rate at 8 MiB with 0, 1 and 2 injected NOPs: 57.2, 64.8 and 69.0 GB/s on CPU 2 and 58.1, 64.7 and 69.5 GB/s on CPU 41 (part N) [Ref10].
  • Prediction P-A5 holds on both CPUs. It said that the L2 long-latency read misses per line at 8 MiB with 2 injected NOPs are below 0.8 times the value with 0 NOPs. They fall from 0.3213 to 0.0005 on CPU 2 and 0.3206 to 0.0006 on CPU 41 [Ref8].
  • With 2 injected NOPs both prefetchers work. At 8 MiB the L1 prefetches per line rise from 0.009 to 0.65 on CPU 2 and 0.009 to 0.69 on CPU 41. The L2 accesses by the L1 prefetcher rise from 0.08 to 0.99 per line (CPU 2).
  • The ASCT loop with 2 injected NOPs then behaves like our new read loop. At 8 MiB on CPU 2 it reads 69.5 GB/s with 2.58 cycles, 0.35 L1 long-latency misses and 0.0005 L2 long-latency misses per line. The new read loop on 2026-11-15: 69.0 GB/s, 2.60 cycles, 0.34 and 0.0005 (median of 2 counted processes of step ZC) [Ref2].
  • Prediction P-A4 holds on both CPUs. It said that a loop which is limited by its own instructions keeps its rate within 3 % from 1 MiB to 8 MiB. With 4 injected NOPs the rate is 34.9 and then 35.5 GB/s on CPU 2 and 35.4 and then 35.5 GB/s on CPU 41. With 8 it is 19.3 and then 18.9 GB/s on CPU 2 and 19.6 and then 19.8 GB/s on CPU 41 [Ref8].
  • Not explained: the spread of the loop with 2 injected NOPs at 1 MiB. Its 4 processes of part N lie within 63.2 to 83.6 GB/s on CPU 2 and 58.2 to 86.7 GB/s on CPU 41. The 6 counted processes of part NC lie within 82.1 to 85.7 GB/s on CPU 2 and 82.2 to 85.5 GB/s on CPU 41. Prediction P-A4 does not cover this loop, because its median at 1 MiB is above 60 GB/s.

• The explanation for the ASCT loop without NOPs at 8 MiB: its loads ask for lines before the prefetchers have fetched them. Prediction P-A5 was the test of this explanation, and it holds.
  • A loop with a slower pace gets its lines into L2 in time. Then it needs about 2.6 cycles per line at 8 MiB, against 1.87 cycles per line at 1 MiB for the fastest loop (ASCT read, 0 NOPs, CPU 2).
  • The handoff of 2026-11-15 reports 73.2 to 73.9 GB/s at 8 MiB for its padded loop read_nop64, and 71.0 to 71.6 GB/s for the upper level of the new read loop [Ref2]. The best ASCT form of this work reads 69.0 and 69.5 GB/s (2 injected NOPs, CPUs 2 and 41).
q1_mesh_intro: The request asked for counters of the SLC, of the mesh and of the hops. The mesh has its own counters (Linux units arm_cmn_0 and arm_cmn_1). Reading them needs root.
mesh_single_missing: The root command for the mesh counters (sudo perf stat -a) was refused by the permission system of this agent session. No mesh counter was read in this work. The run script and its run list are ready (run_mesh.sh, spec_single.txt, sets_single.txt in the folder of [Ref9]). They read 42 mesh events while one core runs the ASCT loop at 1, 6, 8, 12 and 32 MiB and at 1 GiB.
q1_mesh: Three things about the SLC and the mesh are visible from the core counters, without root.

• The SLC holds the whole buffer up to 32 MiB. The counter of last-level read misses (ll_cache_miss_rd) is 0.000 per line at every size up to 32 MiB on both CPUs. It is 0.127 per line at 256 MiB and 0.202 at 1 GiB (CPU 2) [Ref10].
  • The mesh never reports itself busy at 8 MiB. Each answer that a core receives from the mesh carries a busy level from 0 to 3. At 8 MiB the core receives 1.87 answers per line with level 0 and 0.000 with levels 1 to 3 (CPU 2). At 1 GiB it receives 0.40 answers per line with levels 1 to 3.
  • Distance. CPU 2 sits in column 1 of its mesh, which is the outer column of the cores. CPU 41 sits in column 5, near the middle. The mean distance to the 35 SLC slices of the mesh is 4.20 hops for CPU 2 and 3.06 hops for CPU 41 (est., from the kernel map and the inferred core positions) [Ref14]. The ASCT rate of CPU 41 is 1.4 to 1.5 % higher at every size from 4 to 32 MiB. It is 3.0 to 3.5 % higher at 256 MiB and 1 GiB. At 2 MiB and below the two CPUs differ by -0.8 to +0.4 %.

Hypothesis. The shorter mean distance of CPU 41 causes its higher rate above 4 MiB. Two CPUs cannot prove it. The measurement that would confirm or reject it: the same sweep on CPUs at other columns of the mesh.
q1_verdict:
• ASCT confirms the fall at 8 MiB. A load-only loop loses rate when its buffer no longer fits L2. The ASCT loop loses 40 % on CRB and 38 % and 40 % on the two Arm reference machines. So the fall is not an error of our new read loop.
  • ASCT gives no higher rate at 8 MiB than our new read loop. ASCT read: 57.2 GB/s. ASCT read with 2 injected NOPs: 69.0 GB/s. New read: 71.0 GB/s. Old read: 67.0 GB/s (CPU 2).
  • Why the gain is small at 8 MiB. The old read loop is limited by its own work. It needs 2.67 cycles per line at every size from 1 to 16 MiB [Ref2]. A load-only loop is limited by the supply of lines. From L2 a line costs about 1.9 to 2.1 cycles (ASCT read and new read at 1 MiB). At 8 MiB a line costs about 2.5 to 2.6 cycles, also when it is prefetched in time (new read, and ASCT read with 2 injected NOPs). So the two limits are 27 % apart at 1 MiB and a few percent apart at 8 MiB.
  • The prefetchers. No prefetch counter changes its course at 8 MiB (rule R-A3). The prefetchers explain why the ASCT loop is slower than the new read loop at 8 MiB (prediction P-A5). They do not explain the small gain of the new read loop: its lines were in L2 in time on 2026-11-15 (0.0005 L2 long-latency misses per line) [Ref2].

Insufficient data: why a line from the SLC costs about 0.5 to 0.7 cycles more than a line from L2 when it arrives in L2 in time. The measurements that would resolve it: the mesh and SLC counters while one core runs the loop (root), and the prefetch events of this work counted for our own new read loop.
q2_intro: The runs of this section use one thread on each of 120 CPUs: CPUs 0 to 63 on mesh 0 and CPUs 64 to 119 on mesh 1. Each thread has a 256 MiB buffer, so the lines come from memory.

• ASCT read: 6 processes with 0 injected NOPs and 2 processes for each of 15 other NOP counts, measured phase 2 s [Ref9] [Ref10].
  • Check with the ASCT default of 0.25 s: 3 processes with 0 injected NOPs read 234.9 GB/s (range 233.5 to 235.4).
  • Old read and new read: the values of 2026-11-15 on the same 120 CPUs [Ref3]. They were not run again in this work.
  • Load of CRB: before each process the script waited until at most 2 tasks were runnable, and then 5 s. At most 2 tasks were runnable at the start of the 100 processes. No user was logged in. The 1-minute load average at the starts was 0.00 to 61.1. Its high values are the trace of the process before (est.) [Ref10].
  • How ASCT builds its total. Every thread runs the same number of passes and measures its own time. ASCT adds the rates of the threads. When some threads finish early, the others then run with less competition, and the total is too high. So table 5 also gives a lower bound: all bytes of the process divided by the time of its slowest thread [Ref5] [Ref8].
cap_chip: Figure 8. On CRB the ASCT loop without NOPs reads 229.4 GB/s, less than both of our loops. With 10 injected NOPs it reads 622.5 GB/s, more than both. On the two Arm reference machines the ASCT loop reads 583.6 and 650.5 GB/s without NOPs.
cap_nops: Figure 9. On CRB the total rises from 229.4 GB/s at 0 injected NOPs to 622.5 GB/s at 10. From 30 injected NOPs on it falls, because the NOPs become the limit. On the Arm reference machines the total is highest at 0 injected NOPs.
q2_rates:
• Prediction P-B1 holds. It said that the ASCT total at 64+56 with 0 injected NOPs is below 334 GB/s. The median of 6 processes is 229.4 GB/s (range 228.5 to 233.0) [Ref8] [Ref10].
  • Prediction P-B2 holds. It said that at least one NOP count from 1 to 40 gives 459 GB/s or more. 9 counts do by the ASCT total: 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40. 6 counts do by the lower bound: 6, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30 [Ref8].
  • The highest total is 622.5 GB/s at 10 injected NOPs. That is 2.71 times the total without NOPs. The lower bounds are 216.4 and 588.1 GB/s, a factor of 2.72.
  • Mesh 0 becomes fast first. With 4 injected NOPs a thread of mesh 0 reads 5.05 GB/s and a thread of mesh 1 reads 2.75 GB/s (median threads). With 10 injected NOPs they read 5.21 and 5.20 GB/s.
  • Caution for 3 and 4 injected NOPs. The threads of mesh 0 finish in about 2.0 s, and the slowest thread needs 3.9 s. ASCT prints 464.3 and 474.9 GB/s. The lower bounds are 330.8 and 326.1 GB/s.
  • Our loops for comparison. New read: 288.5 to 309.8 GB/s. Old read: 465.5 to 470.1 GB/s. Our loop with one load per line (read_1pl): 230.2 to 235.0 GB/s [Ref3]. The ASCT loop without NOPs also has one load per line. Its 229.4 GB/s is 0.4 to 2.4 % below that loop.
  • The old read loop was not in the fastest state. In its runs of 2026-11-15 a thread of mesh 1 read 2.51 to 2.78 GB/s [Ref3]. That is the rate of a mesh 1 thread of the ASCT loop with 3 or 4 injected NOPs (2.78 and 2.75 GB/s). With 10 injected NOPs a mesh 1 thread reads 5.20 GB/s.
  • Above 30 injected NOPs the NOPs are the limit. The total is 464.3 GB/s at 40, 201.2 GB/s at 100 and 116.6 GB/s at 180.
cap_threads: Figure 10. With 10 injected NOPs one thread reads 2.9 times as much as without NOPs on mesh 0, and 2.6 times as much on mesh 1.
q2_layouts:
• Prediction P-B3 holds. It said that one mesh alone reads within 5 % of its values of 2026-11-15. 64+0 reads 349.1 GB/s (2026-11-15: 348.0 to 351.0). 0+56 reads 319.7 GB/s (2026-11-15: 318.0 to 321.7) [Ref3] [Ref8].
  • One mesh alone is not slow. Without NOPs a thread reads 5.53 GB/s at 64+0 and 5.76 GB/s at 0+56 (median threads). At 64+56 it reads 1.81 and 2.02 GB/s.
  • The slow state needs threads on both meshes, not 120 threads. 56+56 (112 threads) reads 237.8 GB/s without NOPs and 618.3 GB/s with 20 injected NOPs.
  • Count of processes. Each cell of table 6 has 3 or 4 processes. The reason is a defect of the run script, see section 6.
  • Share of the single-mesh sum. 64+0 and 0+56 add up to 668.8 GB/s. 64+56 reaches 34 % of that without NOPs and 93 % with 10 injected NOPs.
q2_cnt_intro: The counted runs use the probe build on all 120 threads. Each of the 7 event sets ran once in each of three cases, with a 2 s measured phase [Ref9] [Ref10].

• 64+56, 0 injected NOPs (slow): the 7 counted processes read 236 to 254 GB/s.
  • 64+56, 20 injected NOPs (fast): 620 to 622 GB/s.
  • 64+0, 0 injected NOPs (one mesh): 351 to 354 GB/s.
  • Table 7 gives each counter per 64-byte line as the median over the threads of a mesh.
q2_cnt:
• Cycles per line. A thread needs 97 cycles per line on mesh 0 and 89 on mesh 1 in the slow case. It needs 34 cycles in the fast case and 32 cycles with one mesh alone.
  • In the fast case no load waits for memory. L2 long-latency read misses: 0.0000 per line. Last-level read misses: 0.0000 per line. Stall cycles for memory: 0.002 per line. The prefetchers fetch every line: 0.90 L1 prefetches and 1.00 L2 accesses by the L1 prefetcher per line.
  • In the slow case 30 % of the loads wait for memory. Last-level read misses: 0.30 per line on both meshes. L1 prefetches: 0.07 per line. Stall cycles for memory: 84 and 78 per line.
  • One mesh alone has almost the same miss pattern and is fast. At 64+0 the last-level read misses are 0.26 per line and the stall cycles for memory 31 per line.
  • A load that waits for memory waits longer when both meshes are loaded. Stall cycles for memory divided by last-level read misses: 277 and 257 cycles in the slow case, 122 cycles with one mesh alone (est., a quotient of two medians).
  • Busy level. In the slow case 62 % of the answers from the mesh carry busy level 0 (mesh 0). In the fast case 4 % do, and with one mesh alone 14 %. So the mesh reports itself less busy in the slow case than in the two faster cases.
  • Not involved. Page-table walks are 0.0000 per line in all three cases. All counters for prefetch instructions are 0.

Hypothesis. The slow state needs two things at the same time: loads that the prefetchers do not cover, and threads on both meshes. The counters support the first part: the slow case has uncovered loads and the fast case has none. They do not show which hardware part makes an uncovered load wait more than twice as long. The measurement that would show it: the mesh counters at 0, 4 and 20 injected NOPs (root).
q2_mesh_intro: The work of 2026-11-15 read 22 sets of mesh counters as root while our loops ran at 64+56. The plan of this work was the same read for the ASCT loop at 0, 4 and 20 injected NOPs.
mesh_chip_missing: The root command for the mesh counters (sudo perf stat -a) was refused by the permission system of this agent session. No mesh counter was read in this work. The run script and its run list are ready (run_mesh.sh, spec_chip.txt, sets_chip.txt in the folder of [Ref9]).
q2_mesh: The mesh counters of 2026-11-15 for the old read loop and the new read loop are in the report of that work [Ref3].
q2_verdict:
• ASCT reproduces the low whole-chip rate. Its own loop reads 229.4 GB/s on the same 120 CPUs. Our new read loop reads 288.5 to 309.8 GB/s [Ref3].
  • The low rate is a state of CRB, not its capacity. The same binary on the same CPUs reads 622.5 GB/s with 10 injected NOPs (lower bound 588.1 GB/s). That is above the old read loop (465.5 to 470.1 GB/s).
  • What goes with the state. The loop without NOPs is slow, and its counters show loads that the prefetchers do not cover. The loop with 20 injected NOPs is fast, and its counters show no such load. This agrees with the result of 2026-11-15, where loops with a long window were slow [Ref3].
  • The Arm reference machines do not show the state. Their totals are highest without NOPs: 583.6 and 650.5 GB/s [Ref11].

Hypothesis. The state belongs to the configuration of CRB: firmware v0.7.2 with one NUMA node. The Arm reference machines run firmware v0.9.0 with two NUMA nodes. The measurement that would confirm or reject it: the same ASCT runs on CRB after a change to firmware v0.9.0.
Insufficient data: which hardware part causes the slow state. The measurement that would resolve it: the mesh counters for the ASCT loop at 0, 4 and 20 injected NOPs (root).
vendor: The Arm welcome kit holds two complete ASCT runs that Arm made on its own machines [Ref11]. They ran through the ASCT front end, as root.

• Machine A0: 128 CPUs, 2 NUMA nodes, firmware v0.9.0, 12 memory channels at 7200 MT/s. Its one-core runs use CPU 63.
  • Machine A1: 136 CPUs, 2 NUMA nodes, firmware v0.9.0, 12 memory channels at 8000 MT/s. Its one-core runs use CPU 67.
  • CRB: 128 CPUs (120 used), 1 NUMA node, firmware v0.7.2, 10 memory modules at 8000 MT/s [Ref12].

• CRB and A0 agree from 4 to 32 MiB. The ASCT rate of CRB CPU 2 differs from A0 by 0.0 to 0.6 % at 4, 8, 16 and 32 MiB. At 8 MiB: 57.21 GB/s on CRB and 57.31 GB/s on A0. So the fall at 8 MiB does not come from the firmware version of CRB.
  • CRB is slower from memory. At 1 GiB the ASCT loop reads 31.9 GB/s on CRB CPU 2 and 32.9 GB/s on CPU 41. It reads 36.1 GB/s on A0 and 36.2 GB/s on A1.

• Without NOPs the Arm machines are 2.5 and 2.8 times as fast as CRB. A0 reads 583.6 GB/s and A1 reads 650.5 GB/s with the CPUs of the whole machine. CRB reads 229.4 GB/s with 120 threads.
  • On the Arm machines every injected NOP costs rate. A0: 583.6, 565.8, 548.6 GB/s at 0, 10 and 20 injected NOPs. CRB: 229.4, 622.5, 619.7 GB/s.
  • Where the NOPs are the limit, the machines agree. At 100 injected NOPs CRB reads 201.2 GB/s with 120 threads and A0 reads 210.4 GB/s. At 180: 116.6 and 121.6 GB/s.
  • Share of the memory channels. ASCT gives a "peak theoretical" rate: channels × transfer rate × 8 bytes. For A0 that is 691.2 GB/s, and ASCT reports 85.0 % for reads. The same formula gives 640 GB/s for the 10 modules of CRB (est., computed here, not printed by ASCT). The CRB total at 10 injected NOPs is 97 % of that, and its lower bound is 92 %.
Other traffic types. The ASCT benchmark peak-bandwidth has four read-write types beside "All Reads". Table 8 gives them for the 120 CPUs of CRB.
vendor2:
• On CRB one type stands out. "1:1 Reads-Writes" reads and writes 480.3 GB/s. The other three types and "All Reads" lie between 170.9 and 242.9 GB/s.
  • On the Arm machines "All Reads" is the highest type.
  • Hypothesis. The four slower types on CRB are in the slow state of section 3, and the 1:1 loop has a slower pace. No counter was captured for these types. The measurement that would confirm or reject it: the counted runs of table 7 for each type.
runs: All runs: CRB, 2026-11-16, after the end of the block that Jeremy Conner had announced for 17:30 to 23:10 UTC [Ref13]. Nine logins: five ran one script each, and four copied result folders.

• 23:12 UTC, preparation (folder asct-prep-20261116T231215Z): machine record, build of the probe binary, event codes, test processes. Load average before the first process: 0.03 0.01 0.00. Users logged in: 0.
  • 23:12 to 23:19 UTC, one core (folder asct-single-20261116T231240Z): 800 processes, 0 with a non-zero exit code. 1-minute load average at the starts: 0.08 to 1.22.
  • 23:19 to 23:33 UTC, whole chip (folder asct-chip-20261116T231956Z): 80 processes, 0 with a non-zero exit code. At most 2 runnable tasks at a start.
  • 23:37 UTC, one core with injected NOPs and counters (folder asct-single-20261116T233721Z): 72 processes, 0 with a non-zero exit code. 1-minute load average at the starts: 1.14 to 1.25.
  • 23:44 to 23:47 UTC, whole chip, two steps again (folder asct-chip-20261116T234426Z): 20 processes, 0 with a non-zero exit code.
  • Checks of the counters: every counter row ran for the whole time that it was enabled, and that time is within 2 % of the measured phase of its thread. Rows that fail: 0 [Ref10].
  • Shared machine: Slack channel #phoenix-crb was read at 23:12, 23:19, 23:23, 23:32, 23:37 and 23:44 UTC. That is before every script and twice during the whole-chip run. No new block was announced. Every script checks the marker file of the other user (/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING) before every process. It was never present.
  • CPUs: only CPUs 0 to 119. Nothing ran on CPUs 120 to 127.
  • Root: not used for any run. The preparation script ran sudo -n true once, to test whether sudo asks for a password. No setting of CRB was changed. No package was installed.
  • Files on CRB: ~/cache-perf/asct-20261116/ (scripts, the build folder, the probe binary) and 5 folders ~/cache-perf/results/asct-*.

• Mesh counters were not captured. The root command for the mesh counters (sudo perf stat -a) was refused by the permission system of this agent session. No mesh counter was read in this work. The request asked for them.
  • A defect of the whole-chip script overwrote 8 result files. The function that starts a process used the same variable name as the loop that numbers the processes. In the steps for the other layouts and for the traffic types the second process of 8 cells got the file name of the first. The script was corrected, and both steps ran again at 23:44 UTC. Tables 6 and 8 use every result file that exists: 3 or 4 processes per cell [Ref9] [Ref10].
  • The counted whole-chip processes without NOPs read more than the uncounted ones. Counted: 236 to 254 GB/s. Uncounted: 228.5 to 233.0 GB/s. The cause was not examined.
  • Three additions after data was seen: part NC, the lower bound for the totals, and the list of mesh runs. Each is recorded with its time in the decisions file [Ref8].
  • Old read and new read were not run again. Their values are one day older than the ASCT values.
  • Another account on CRB. The process list of 23:19:56 UTC shows a session-manager process (systemd) of another account with 3.1 % CPU share. No user was logged in at any start of a process, and the marker file was absent [Ref10].
  • No review by a second person or agent. The scripts were tested on the development machine with stand-in binaries before the first login.
open:
• Mesh, SLC and hop counters for the ASCT loop. They need an approval of a read-only root command on CRB (sudo perf stat -a on the units arm_cmn_0 and arm_cmn_1). The scripts and run lists are ready [Ref9]. Run time: about 20 minutes (est.).
  • Registers. ASCT can read core registers only with a kernel module that CRB does not have, and its mesh register report needs root and /dev/mem. A statement from Arm on the prefetcher settings of firmware v0.7.2 would also answer it.
  • Firmware. The Arm reference machines with firmware v0.9.0 and two NUMA nodes do not show the slow whole-chip state. The same ASCT runs on CRB after a firmware change would show whether the firmware is the cause.
  • Prefetch counters for our own loops. This work counted the prefetch events for the ASCT loop only. The same 7 event sets for the old and the new read loop would complete table 4.
  • The two rates of the new read loop at 8 MiB stay open from 2026-11-15. The ASCT loop shows one rate.
  • The spread of the ASCT loop with 2 injected NOPs at 1 MiB (58 to 87 GB/s between processes) is not explained.
subtitle: CRB is the Arm Phoenix Reference Server in our lab. ASCT is the Arm System Characterization Tool, version 0.7.1+77461b3. Runs of 2026-11-16, 23:12 to 23:47 UTC. Page built from facts.json by report.py.
short:
• 8 MiB on one core. The read loop of ASCT also loses rate from 1 MiB to 8 MiB (95.9 to 57.2 GB/s on CPU 2), and no form of it reads 8 MiB faster than our new read loop (69.0 against 71.0 GB/s).
  • Whole chip. On the same 120 CPUs the ASCT loop reads 229.4 GB/s, and with 10 injected delay rounds it reads 622.5 GB/s, so the low whole-chip number is a state of CRB and not its capacity.
  • Counters. In both slow cases the core counters show loads that run ahead of the hardware prefetchers, and the mesh counters are missing, because the root command for them was refused in this session.
